extracted.intended_audience: architects, artists, art historians, and students of design interested in Gothic architecture and principles of artistic composition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for Gothic architecture and general artistic composition, emphasizing variety, naturalism, the roles of craft freedom, and the balance of fact and design. Useful for critics, designers, and students assessing or producing architectural/artistic work in the Gothic spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of the workman (craftsman liberty)
rubrics_metrics.description: In design and execution, the workman must have been altogether set free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The artisan's liberty allows true invention and variation; enforced adherence to fixed forms (legal forms) converts architecture into manufacture. Anti-pattern: forcing builders to produce 'proper' forms only (e.g., fixed capitals) prevents creative, living architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between love of order and love of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Love of order (desire for matching symmetry and fixed forms) is useful in commerce and practical matters but is not the same as love of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order is necessary in its highest sense for art, but mere punctuality and methodical habits do not guarantee perception of creative powers. Anti-pattern: confusing administrative or commercial order with artistic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / novelty as essential merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Great art, whether in words, colors, or stones, does not say the same thing over and over again; the merit of architecture (and every art) consists in its saying new and different things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition/strict conformity to models is manufacture, not art. Requirement: architects should be not only correct but entertaining. Example: copying capitals from Phidias is less rational than true inventive work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture should entertain as well as be correct
rubrics_metrics.description: We may require of an architect, as we do of a novelist, that he should be not only correct, but entertaining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buildings should provide delight beyond mere convenience, symmetry, or workmanship. Anti-pattern: producing structures that satisfy technical correctness but give no imaginative or emotional pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of slavish rule- or model-based practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Exactly so far as architecture works on known rules, and from given models, it is not an art, but a manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using fixed 'orders' or one 'proper' form for elements (capitals, mouldings) reduces the work to copying. Good architecture requires inventive adaptation, not blind replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of variety/change in composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Change or variety is as much a necessity to the human heart and brain in buildings as in books; there is no merit in mere monotony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architecture should avoid uniform ornaments and proportions; variety provides pleasure and reflects living thought. Analogy: variety in nature (clouds, trees) is desirable; monotony is analogous to an unvarying universe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced use of monotony and change
rubrics_metrics.description: Monotony has sublimity and use, but after a certain degree it becomes uninteresting or intolerable; the composer breaks monotony either by enriching repeated passages or by introducing new passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architectural composition should employ monotony to give value to change; the observer needs patience to endure monotony to appreciate the subsequent change. Example: musical structure and sea-waves illustrate healthy relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patience of the beholder as a condition of reward
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to the enjoyment of change, a certain degree of patience is required from the hearer or observer; endurance of monotony is a price paid for future pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers may legitimately include long or grave monotony that demands audience patience; audiences with 'strong intellect' will accept and derive high pleasure from this endurance. Scoring note: works that demand patience may be judged for depth rather than immediate appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Healthy vs diseased love of change
rubrics_metrics.description: A healthy love of change admits subtle variation and intermingling with noble monotony; a diseased love of change repeats change too often until change itself becomes monotonous, driving one to extreme and fantastic degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether variety is tasteful and tempered (healthy) or excessive and fatiguing (diseased). Gothic in best schools shows subtle & delicate change; barbaric schools show fantastic redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotony used instrumentally (transparent monotony)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monotony, used to give value to change, particularly that transparent monotony like the shadows of a great painter, is essential in architectural composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monotony should allow dimly suggested forms to be seen through it; used properly it enhances later changes. Anti-pattern: constant monotony that is deadening rather than preparatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gothic capacity for perpetual novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic invented forms (pointed arch, grouped shaft, tracery) the merit of which was not just novelty but the capacity for perpetual novelty—admitting millions of variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate Gothic elements for their inherent variability and adaptability; the pointed arch's changeable proportions are a positive virtue compared to fixed circular arches. Scoring: preference for forms that allow endless, coherent variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability and fitness to service
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic is that which can fit itself most easily to all services, vulgar or noble: undefined in slope, height, breadth, disposition; it can shrink into a turret or expand into a hall with grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good architectural style should submit to functional changes without loss of unity or majesty. Anti-pattern: styles that force arbitrary symmetry at the expense of utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding external symmetry when it hinders use
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic builders never suffered ideas of outside symmetries and consistencies to interfere with the real use and value of what they did.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical needs (opening windows, adding rooms, building buttresses) should override rigid demands for formal correspondence; such daring interruptions often increase interest rather than injure symmetry. Example: differing towers on cathedral fronts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety may be distributed across features
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety in Gothic design manifests variably: if mouldings are constant, surface sculpture will change; if capitals are fixed, traceries will vary, and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a work, look across features for compensatory variation; a perceived monotony in one element may be balanced by novelty in another. Scoring: a holistic view of variation across elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture as confession of imperfection and desire of change
rubrics_metrics.description: The first two elements of good architecture are the confession of Imperfection and the confession of Desire of Change; buildings should not assert perfect or final satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A human building should express restlessness and progression (love of change) rather than finality; anti-pattern: works that claim absolute perfection ('And behold, it was very good').

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalism: frank representation of natural objects
rubrics_metrics.description: The love of natural objects for their own sake, and the effort to represent them frankly, unconstrained by artistical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When craftsmen are left free they look to nature for material and represent it with varying accuracy and fancy. Distinction: Western (Gothic) delights in representation of facts; Eastern delights in harmony of colors/forms. Anti-patterns: slavish imitation that destroys composition, or fantastical invention that ignores facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between composition (abstract arrangement) and representation of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrangement of colors and lines (composition) is analogous to music and independent of representation of facts; good coloring/abstract form does not necessarily convey likeness to anything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noblest art unites abstract composition with imitative power, but most artists fall into specialization. Evaluation should note whether a work successfully balances abstract relations with truthful representation or errs toward one extreme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three artistic types: men of facts, men of design, and central men
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists are divided into three classes: on the right, men of facts; on the left, men of design; in the centre, men of both. Each class has healthy functions and potential diseases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the artist's or work's alignment: fact-oriented works aim for truthful representation; design-oriented works aim for noble composition; central works attempt both. Scoring: central works (both facts and design) are highest, though each class has value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disease 1: men of facts despise design
rubrics_metrics.description: When men of facts despise design, they suppose perfect imitation or sympathy with nature is all that is required, leading to deadness of feeling and inability to admire great designers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: imitative painters who refuse to study composition and deride composition-based works. Impact: such attitudes can damage broader artistic appreciation and lead to iconoclasm against non-factual art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disease 2: men of design despise facts
rubrics_metrics.description: When men of design despise facts, they neglect truths of nature in favor of invention, producing decor that lacks natural vitality (example: some Chinese ornament).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good design must draw on natural facts to remain vital; anti-pattern: fanciful invention that ignores natural reference resulting in lifeless ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disease 3: men of facts envy design (plagiarism/law-of-art worship)
rubrics_metrics.description: When men of facts envy design they try to acquire inventive powers by slavishly copying reputed designers, resulting in plagiarism and useless work that deceives by base resemblances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: imitators trained only in the rules of composition who produce fungous growths of imitation; historically a major error leading to sterile art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disease 4: men of design envy facts (over-imitative ornament)
rubrics_metrics.description: When men of design envy facts, they attempt close imitation of nature and lose ornamental function and compositional power (e.g., hawthorn moulding painted green).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance required: ornament should not sacrifice composition in a bid for graphic truth. Anti-pattern: excessive literalism in ornament that weakens the overall design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative danger of morbid conditions: facts-type disorders more harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: The morbid conditions of men of facts (despising or envying design) are more dangerous and harmful to society than the morbid conditions of men of design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the social and cultural impact of the work's orientation: fact-only movements can become destructive (iconoclasm, refusal of design), whereas design-only morbidities mainly impair the designers themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search after whole truth (good and evil) as highest aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists, considered as searchers after truth, should perceive and pursue both the good and the evil (the whole thing as it verily is); central artists do this, whereas right-only perceive and pursue the good and left-only pursue the evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highest artistic achievement involves truthful perception of the full complexity of nature/fact, not selective or perverse emphasis. Assessment should favor works that honestly engage both positive and negative aspects of their subjects.
